newsitem.title: USA: Chicago columnist Mike Royko dies at 64.
newsitem.headline: Chicago columnist Mike Royko dies at 64.

text.p: Mike Royko, whose columns deflated the powerful and celebrated the everyday men and women of Chicago for 35 years, died Tuesday after suffering a brain aneurysm one week ago. He was 64.

The Pulitzer Prize-winning writer died at Northwestern Memorial Hospital where he had undergone surgery last Wednesday, the hospital said. It listed the cause of death as heart failure and said funeral arrangements were pending.
His death silenced one of the country's most recognised newspaper voices, one that spoke to readers day after day with satire and clarity in publications big and small across the United States.
"He didn't pull any punches," said Chicago Sun-Times columnist Irv Kupcinet.

"There was only one Mike Royko," added Sam Sianis, in whose Billy Goat Tavern beneath Michigan Avenue Royko on many evenings drew inspirations and sometimes a setting for his essays. "My heart is broken ... people like that, they come once in a century."

Royko had suffered a stroke earlier in the year while vacationing in Florida and had also undergone surgery there for an aneurysm. He collapsed last Tuesday at his home in Winnetka north of Chicago and emergency personnel said his heart had stopped beating for several minutes.
He was later moved to Northwestern Hospital in downtown Chicago for last week's surgery.

Royko was born in Chicago in 1932 of Polish and Ukrainian parentage, growing up with gritty ethnic characters who would later populate his column under fictional names, passing judgment on the puffery, venality and pretense of politicians, crooks and high society.

He had worked for the Chicago Tribune since 1984, jumping there from the rival Chicago Sun-Times which he left after Rupert Murdoch bought the newspaper. He began his career in 1956 at the City News Bureau, a grass roots news-gathering operation run jointly by Chicago's newspapers.

He joined the now defunct Chicago Daily News in 1959 and began a once-a-week column at that newspaper in 1962, becoming a full-time columnist there two years later until that newspaper folded. It was at the Daily News that he won the Pulitzer in 1972.

His career was not without controversy. One column he wrote a few years infuritated Chicago's Hispanic community and resulted in a mass demonstration in front of the Tribune building. The demonstrators were outraged at language they said was demeaning.
His book "Boss" was hailed as a definitive portrait of the late Mayor Richard J. Daley, father of the city's current mayor, Richard M. Daley.
In last Sunday's edition of the Tribune, colleague James Warren of the newspaper's Washington bureau noted that Royko's column had found its way into about 800 newwspapers.
He quoted some small-town editors who said their readers almost thought of Royko as the man down the street, not a writer in a far-off city.
"To be in 100 or 200 (newspapers) is darm good," Warren wrote. "And for 30 years he did five columns a weeek, whereas most struggle to do two."
